quests.explanation: The suffix '-ance' turns a verb into a noun describing a result or amount, as in 'allow' becoming 'allowance.'
Like 'allowance,' this noun is formed by adding '-ance' to a verb, describing what is passed down or received.
The suffix '-ship' describes a state or condition, as in 'friendship' and 'relationship' — both describing a connection between people.
The prefix 'grand-' adds one generation back in family words, as in 'grandparent,' 'grandchild,' and 'grandmother.'
This compound word describes everyone and everything 'held' together within one house — a useful memory link.
The suffix '-hood' describes a state or period of life, as in 'childhood,' 'adulthood,' and 'neighborhood.'
Like 'station' and 'vacation,' this word ends in the common noun suffix '-tion,' always pronounced 'shun.'
The prefix 'pre-' means 'before,' and 'scription' relates to writing — a prescription is literally something written beforehand by a doctor.
This word comes from Greek 'allos' (other) and 'ergon' (work) — the body reacting in an 'other' way to something harmless.

quests.hint: Remember the 'mp' cluster — every letter here is pronounced: SYMP-TOM.
quests.explanation: Unlike words with truly silent letters, every letter in 'symptom' is pronounced, even though the 'mp' cluster can feel tricky to say.
Adding '-y' to the verb 'recover' forms the noun, following the same pattern as 'discover' to 'discovery.'
The suffix '-ment' turns the verb 'treat' into a noun describing the process or method of treating something.

quests.hint: Remember the 'ph' makes an 'f' sound: PHAR-MA-CY.
quests.explanation: The 'ph' spelling for the 'f' sound comes from Greek, appearing in many medical and scientific words like 'pharmacy' and 'phase.'
This word comes from Latin 'vita' (life) plus 'amine,' since vitamins were first thought to all contain amine compounds essential to life.
The suffix '-ness' turns an adjective into a noun describing a state, as in 'well' becoming 'wellness' and 'happy' becoming 'happiness.'

quests.hint: Tricky letters: OR-CHES-TRA, with 'ch' sounding like 'k.'
quests.explanation: Borrowed from Greek, 'orchestra' keeps the Greek 'ch' spelling pronounced as 'k,' a pattern shared with words like 'chorus' and 'echo.'
The root 'audi' relates to hearing (as in 'audio'), so an audience is literally a group gathered to listen.
The prefix 're-' means 'again,' so a rehearsal is literally a repeated practice before the real performance.
Despite looking related to 'cost' (price), 'costume' actually comes from a different root meaning 'custom' or 'habit' of dress.
The root 'spect' means 'to look' (as in 'inspect' and 'respect'), so a spectator is literally 'one who looks' at an event.
This word comes from Latin 'itinerarium,' meaning 'a journey' — a useful link for remembering both spelling and meaning.
The root 'destine' relates to fate or purpose, so a destination is literally the place you're 'meant' to end up.
The prefix 'ex-' means 'out,' and 'cursion' relates to running — an excursion is literally a trip 'running out' from home.
This frequently misspelled word doubles two different consonants — remembering both doubles together helps avoid the common error of missing one.
The verb 'board' (to get on a plane, train, or ship) simply adds '-ing' with no spelling changes.
The suffix '-ure' turns the verb 'depart' into a noun describing the act of leaving, similar to 'fail' becoming 'failure.'
Money that's 'currently' in circulation gives 'currency' its name and its spelling connection to 'current.'
Borrowed directly from French (meaning 'to remember'), 'souvenir' keeps its original spelling pattern rather than an anglicized one.
A landmark is literally something that 'marks' a notable spot on the 'land,' making this compound word easy to picture and spell.
The prefix 'trans-' means 'across,' so transportation is literally the act of carrying something 'across' a distance.
